one_liner: Embeddable C WebAssembly interpreter (tail-call threaded, register-TOS); first-party CoreMark 2.5x WAMR fast-interp, 1.2x wasm3 on Windows.
what_it_does: KinoWASM is a WebAssembly runtime library in C (a CMake static library, KinoWASM.lib) for embedding in host applications, plus a KinoRuntime CLI with test and measurement drivers. The C API loads modules from a file or memory into a store, looks up and invokes exports, registers host imports in a global table, and lets a host function suspend the guest so the host can call kinowasm_resume later, for example on the next game frame. It is not an API drop-in for WAMR or wasm3: the host has to supply an allocation arena and a linear-memory backend (a Windows one is provided in host/).
how_it_is_fast: At load time each function is translated from the Wasm stack machine into direct-threaded bytecode in which handler function pointers are embedded inline. The translator simulates the operand stack, so local.get and constants are emitted lazily and binary operations come in slot/slot, slot/register and slot/immediate variants. The top of stack lives in a register (r0), and pc, sp, memory base and r0 are passed as the four Win64 register arguments. Every handler ends in a guaranteed tail call ([[msvc::musttail]] or clang musttail), so there is no central dispatch loop. Superinstructions fuse compare+br_if, binop+local.set and the hot i32 load+local.set pairs, and branch targets are resolved to absolute bytecode addresses, so no label stack exists at run time.
when_to_use: Embedding Wasm in a game or engine where JIT is not allowed (the README cites Switch, Switch 2, PS5 and Xbox builds, which are private) and an interpreter is required.
You need cooperative execution: a host import suspends the guest and the main thread resumes it later (Unity Update or Unreal Tick), without Asyncify or worker threads.

A Windows x64 host whose interpreter throughput on scalar integer code is the bottleneck: first-party CoreMark 4,386 iterations/s against 3,556 for wasm3 and 1,734 for the WAMR fast interpreter on an i7-13700F.

You need broad core-spec coverage in an interpreter: tail calls, multi-value, multiple memories, exception handling and wide arithmetic, with a self-reported snapshot of 45,037 passed and 0 failed on the pinned spec suite (2026-09-30).
when_not_to_use: Linux, macOS or ARM hosts: the public build targets only Windows x64 with AVX2 and BMI, and the console ports are not public.
Modules that need SIMD or relaxed SIMD, threads or atomics, GC or typed function references (call_ref), or full WASI: none of these execute.
Peak throughput: any JIT or AOT engine (wasmtime, WAMR AOT, DTVM) will be much faster than this interpreter.

Untrusted or multi-tenant code: the project claims no security audit, runtime state such as g_rt and the host-import registry are process-global and single-thread by design, and the docs tell you to synchronize use of global state yourself.
Risk-averse production dependencies: first commit 2026-09-30, 6 commits, one author, 0 stars, and correctness fixes on 2026-10-08/09.

integration.form: static lib (KinoWASM.lib, C) plus the KinoRuntime CLI; reference host layer in host/ to adapt
integration.dependencies: none for the core library; the host must supply a system arena and a linear-memory backend (Windows reference in host/kw_core_mem_backend_win.h and host/systemmemory.c); wabt and Git only for generating tests
integration.min_toolchain: C11 (/std:c11 for clang-cl, /std:clatest for MSVC); MSVC 14.50+ or clang-cl for guaranteed tail calls (configure fails otherwise); CMake 4.2+ and Ninja
integration.platforms: Windows x64 with AVX2 (and BMI for clang-cl) in the public repository; console builds exist privately according to the README
integration.thread_safety: Not thread-safe: the execution engine keeps runtime state in globals (g_rt, suspension state) on the assumption of a single thread, and the import registry is global; Public-API.md says to synchronize use of global state instead of assuming separate stores are isolated.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — it runs the same .wasm/WASI command-line modules as iwasm and wasm3 through its CLI, but the embedding API is its own (kinowasm_init, kinowasm_load_module, kinowasm_invoke, kinowasm_resume) and needs a host memory backend

gotchas: The CoreMark iteration mismatch is not a harness flaw: CoreMark's auto-calibration (core_main.c multiplies by 10 until a run exceeds 1 s, then by 1 + 10 / seconds) gives 30,000 iterations for iwasm (10,000 took about 5.8 s) and 60,000 for wasm3 and KinoRuntime (about 2.8 s and 2.3 s), which also explains the differing final CRCs. The standard performance-run CRCs (crclist 0xe714, crcmatrix 0x1fd7, crcstate 0x8e3a) appear in all logs.

The baselines are probably handicapped Windows builds of unknown configuration. WAMR's core/config.h enables labels-as-values dispatch only under __GNUC__, so an MSVC or clang-cl iwasm falls back to switch dispatch. wasm3's own docs/Performance.md (2019-2020 figures) shows fib(40) at 5.35 s on Windows 10 against 3.83 s on Linux on the same i5-8250U, a 1.4x gap about the size of KinoRuntime's 1.41x fib lead over wasm3.

The runtimes used different clocks. The iwasm and wasm3 CoreMark times are exact multiples of 1/64 s (1107/64 and 1080/64 s, the 15.6 ms Windows tick), while KinoRuntime reads QueryPerformanceCounter and maps the process and thread CPU-time clocks to that monotonic wall clock. On 13-17 s runs this changes scores by under 0.2%, so it is not a material bias.

The numbers arrived with the first commit (2026-09-30), before the 2026-10-08/09 fixes (live registers below wide-arithmetic operands, integer overflow in buffer-read bounds checks, stale resume state after traps), so the measured binary is not HEAD; Clang 11 CoreMark and the emcc -O2 fib module emit no wide-arithmetic ops. The CoreMark-trained PGO presets are MSVC-only (CMake skips PGO for Clang), so the reported 'standard Clang build' was not PGO-trained, but source comments show code alignment and inlining were tuned against CoreMark.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over wasman (Go, beats the wazero interpreter) or the WasmKit register interpreter (Swift) when the host is C/C++ on Windows or consoles and you need host-driven suspend/resume; pick DTVM or another JIT instead whenever native code generation is allowed and throughput matters more than embedding constraints.
verified_claims_summary: On one Intel Core i7-13700F under Windows 11, user-supplied logs show a CoreMark 1.0 WASI module (Clang 11.0.0 -O3, size 666) scoring 4,385.7 iterations/s in KinoRuntime against 3,555.6 for wasm3 and 1,734.4 for iwasm in WAMR fast-interpreter mode (about 1.23x and 2.53x), and an emcc -O2 recursive fibonacci(40) taking 1,838.9 ms against 2,601.1 and 4,298.9 ms, timed in-guest through each runtime's WASI clock. Runtime versions, the compilers and flags used to build the runtimes, and module hashes are not recorded, and CoreMark is not bundled.
status_note: Active but brand new (first commit 2026-09-30, last 2026-10-09, single author, 0 stars); MIT-licensed C that you can vendor, though the public build covers only Windows x64 and the claimed console production use cannot be checked.
